Accessed September 4, 2014. |website = {{nowrap|{{URL|https://www.franklintwpnj.org}}}} |footnotes = }} '''Franklin Township''' is a [[Township (New Jersey)|township]] in [[Somerset County, New Jersey|Somerset County]], in the [[U.S. state]] of [[New Jersey]]. It is centrally located in the [[Raritan River|Raritan Valley region]] within the [[New York Metropolitan Area]]. As of the [[2020 United States census]], the township's population was 68,364, an increase of 6,064 (+9.7%) from the [[2010 United States census|2010 census]] count of 62,300, which in turn reflected an increase of 11,397 (+22.4%) from the 50,903 counted in the [[2000 United States census|2000 census]].[https://www.nj.gov/labor/labormarketinformation/assets/PDFs/census/2010/2010data/table7cm.xls Table 7. Population for the Counties and Municipalities in New Jersey: 1990, 2000 and 2010], [[New Jersey Department of Labor and Workforce Development]], February 2011. Accessed May 1, 2023. The township was [[List of municipalities in New Jersey|the state's 19th most-populous municipality]] in 2020, after being ranked 22nd in 2010.[https://www.nj.gov/labor/labormarketinformation/assets/PDFs/census/2020/2020%20pl94%20Tables/2020_PL94_Summary/Table_1_2020.xlsx Table1. New Jersey Counties and Most Populous Cities and Townships: 2020 and 2010 Censuses], [[New Jersey Department of Labor and Workforce Development]]. Accessed December 1, 2022. Traditionally a farming community, it has become a fast-growing suburb with massive development in the late 20th and early 21st centuries, fostering a diverse blend of races, religions, and cultures. In 2008, Franklin Township ranked #5 on ''[[Money (magazine)|Money]]'' magazine's list of America's Top 100 Best Places to Live.[https://web.archive.org/web/20080717042019/http://money.cnn.com/magazines/moneymag/bplive/2008/snapshots/CS3424900.html #5 – Franklin Township; America's Top 100 Best Places to Live], ''[[Money (magazine)|Money]]''. Accessed February 12, 2013. What is now Franklin Township was originally formed circa 1745 as [[Eastern precinct, Somerset County, New Jersey|Eastern precinct]]. Franklin Township was incorporated on February 21, 1798, as one of New Jersey's initial group of 104 townships by an act of the [[New Jersey Legislature]]. Portions of the township were taken to form [[South Bound Brook, New Jersey|South Bound Brook]] (formed within Township, became an independent municipality as of April 11, 1907) and [[East Millstone, New Jersey|East Millstone]] (formed on February 18, 1873, and returned to Franklin Township on December 31, 1949).Snyder, John P. [https://www.state.nj.us/dep/njgs/enviroed/oldpubs/bulletin67.pdf ''The Story of New Jersey's Civil Boundaries: 1606-1968''], Bureau of Geology and Topography; Trenton, New Jersey; 1969. p. 223. Accessed October 28, 2012. == History == It has been unclear if the township was named for founding father [[Benjamin Franklin]] or for his illegitimate son [[William Franklin]], a [[Loyalist (American Revolution)|Loyalist]] and the last [[List of Governors of New Jersey|Royal Governor of New Jersey]] (from 1763 to 1776). In 2000, after considering the evidence set forth by [[William B. Brahms]] in his books ''Images of America: Franklin Township'' (1997)[[William B. Brahms|Brahms, William B.]], Images of America: Franklin Township, [[Arcadia Publishing]]; {{ISBN|0-7524-0938-7}} and ''Franklin Township, Somerset County, NJ: A History'',[[William B. Brahms|Brahms, William B.]], ''Franklin Township, Somerset County, NJ: A History'', FTPL; {{ISBN|0-9668586-0-3}} and ''The Case for William Franklin and The Case for Benjamin Franklin'', the Township Council chose the theory that the township was indeed named for Benjamin Franklin.[https://www.franklintwpnj.org/about-franklin/history History] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191014190121/https://www.franklintwpnj.org/about-franklin/history |date=October 14, 2019 }}, Township of Franklin. Accessed March 31, 2020. "After considering the evidence set forth in Franklin Township, Somerset County, NJ: A History, William B. Brahm, Commissioned by the Franklin Township Library, 1998, Chapter 12, Municipal Government, The Case for William Franklin and The Case for Benjamin Franklin, the Township Council determined to espouse the theory that the Township was named for Benjamin Franklin."Hutchinson, Viola L. [http://mapmaker.rutgers.edu/356/nj_place_names_origin.pdf#page=14 ''The Origin of New Jersey Place Names''], New Jersey Public Library Commission, May 1945. Accessed August 31, 2015. Franklin Township was very much a part of [[American Revolutionary War|Revolutionary War]] history and the scene of many raiding parties along [[New Jersey Route 27|Route 27]], then known as the King's Highway. Two British generals, [[Charles Cornwallis, 1st Marquess Cornwallis|Cornwallis]] and DeHeister, tried to lure [[General]] [[George Washington]] and his [[Continental Army]] into battle on the plains of [[Middlebush, New Jersey|Middlebush]] and [[East Millstone, New Jersey|East Millstone]]. Washington, however, kept his troops at Chimney Rock, just north of Franklin, until the British withdrew. Several of the prosperous Middlebush farms were destroyed by the British soldiers during their retreat. In 1777, near the mill on the [[Millstone River]] at [[Weston, New Jersey|Weston]], the Continental Army and local militia engaged and successfully drove off a British foraging party of about 600 troops, sent out of [[New Brunswick, New Jersey|New Brunswick]] by General Cornwallis.{{fact|date=October 2025}} On November 2, 1783, Washington composed his farewell address to the army while staying at [[Rockingham (house)|Rockingham]] near [[Rocky Hill, New Jersey|Rocky Hill]].{{cite web |last1=Washington |first1=George |author-link=George Washington |title=Washington's Farewell Address to the Army, 2 November 1783 |url=https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Washington/99-01-02-12012 |publisher=[[National Archives and Records Administration|Founders Online, National Archives]] |date=November 2, 1783}} The construction of the [[Delaware and Raritan Canal]] in the 1830s, stretching {{convert|22|mi}} to connect [[New York City]] and [[Philadelphia]], led to significant growth in the township, with as much as 200,000 tons of goods shipped on barges using the canal by the 1860s. The rise of shipping commercial goods using railroads led to a substantial decline in canal traffic.[https://www.franklintwpnj.org/about-franklin/history History] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191014190121/https://www.franklintwpnj.org/about-franklin/history |date=October 14, 2019 }}, Township of Franklin. Accessed March 31, 2020. The area has been restored as the [[Delaware and Raritan Canal State Park]][https://www.dandrcanal.com/history History]. Accessed March 31, 2020. The [[Van Wickle House]], located next to the [[Delaware and Raritan Canal]] in the Somerset section of the township, in between [[New Brunswick, New Jersey|New Brunswick]] and [[South Bound Brook, New Jersey|South Bound Brook]], was built in 1722 by [[Dutch people|Dutch]] settlers and is now owned by Franklin Township and leased by the [[Meadows Foundation (New Jersey)|Meadows Foundation]]. Set back behind Easton Avenue, the home adjoins the [[Rutgers Preparatory School]] and a [[American Revolutionary War|Revolutionary War]]-era graveyard.[http://www.themeadowsfoundation.org/van-wickle-house-1722/ Van Wickle House 1722], Meadows Foundation. Accessed March 31, 2020. Passenger and freight railroad service was available in Franklin Township during the later half of the 19th century via the [[Millstone and New Brunswick Railroad]] (M&NB) which opened in 1854. The railroad was built and operated by the [[Pennsylvania Railroad]] (PRR), from a junction with the PRR mainline at Jersey Avenue in [[New Brunswick, New Jersey|New Brunswick]] to [[East Millstone, New Jersey|East Millstone]]. The M&NB is now known as the [[Conrail]] Millstone Secondary Branch. The branch line was still operated by Conrail up to just west of Clyde Road in [[Somerset, New Jersey|Somerset]] for a time, serving local industry in the industrial section of Somerset.[http://www.eclipse.net/~cobrandt/millston.html A pictorial account concerning the current condition and history of the Millstone Branch] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061201172758/http://www.eclipse.net/~cobrandt/millston.html |date=December 1, 2006 }} As of 2011, Hermann Warehouse Corp re-located out of the Clyde Road facility and there has not been rail service into that building since then.{{fact|date=October 2025}} A bumper was placed east of the [[New Jersey Route 27|Somerset Road/Route 27]] crossing, with Clyde Road, Veronica Avenue and Route 27 crossings currently out of service.{{fact|date=October 2025}} [[New Jersey Route 91|Jersey Avenue/Route 91]] remains the sole active crossing on the line.{{fact|date=October 2025}} In 1922, the infamous [[Hall-Mills Murder]] took place in Franklin Township, in the area adjacent to New Brunswick known as Somerset.[http://mapmaker.rutgers.edu/NorthBrunswick/oldnorthbrunswick.html The Changing Landscape of North Brunswick], [[Rutgers University]]. Accessed February 12, 2013. "Yorston is best remembered for his work in removing the 520 bodies from the New Brunswick Presbyterian Church's cemetery to Van Liew Cemetery to make way for new construction, for his around-the-clock service during the 1918 deadly influenza epidemic, and for his service in connection with the autopsy involving the infamous Hall-Mills murder in neighboring Franklin Township." ==Geography== According to the [[United States Census Bureau]], the township had a total area of 46.88 square miles (121.43 km2), including 46.17 square miles (119.58 km2) of land and 0.71 square miles (1.85 km2) of water (1.52%). The community is approximately 75% rural.Cheslow, Jerry. [https://www.nytimes.com/1998/11/15/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-living-franklin-township-nj-town-acting-preserve-its-farmland.html "If You're Thinking of Living In Franklin Township, N.J.; A Town Acting to Preserve Its Farmland"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', November 15, 1998. Accessed August 23, 2012. "The 47-square-mile community, which is still three-fourths rural, is coming under increasing development pressure, according to Mayor Bottcher." [[2010 United States census]] counted 62,300 people, 23,301 households, and 15,938 families in the township. The [[population density]] was {{convert|1350.0|/sqmi}}. There were 24,426 housing units at an average density of {{convert|529.3|/sqmi}}. The racial makeup was 44.76% (27,887) [[White (U.S. census)|White]], 26.55% (16,539) [[Black (U.S. census)|Black or African American]], 0.29% (183) [[Native American (U.S. census)|Native American]], 19.98% (12,450) [[Asian (U.S. census)|Asian]], 0.01% (9) [[Pacific Islander (U.S. census)|Pacific Islander]], 5.11% (3,183) from [[Race and ethnicity in the United States census|other races]], and 3.29% (2,049) from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. census)|Hispanic or Latino]] of any race were 12.92% (8,050) of the population. Of the 23,301 households, 30.7% had children under the age of 18; 53.3% were married couples living together; 11.2% had a female householder with no husband present and 31.6% were non-families. Of all households, 25.7% were made up of individuals and 8.3% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.63 and the average family size was 3.19. 22.1% of the population were under the age of 18, 7.4% from 18 to 24, 30.4% from 25 to 44, 26.4% from 45 to 64, and 13.7% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 38.3 years. For every 100 females, the population had 92.0 males. For every 100 females ages 18 and older there were 88.5 males. The Census Bureau's 2006–2010 [[American Community Survey]] showed that (in 2010 [[inflation adjustment|inflation-adjusted]] dollars) [[median household income]] was $89,992 (with a margin of error of +/− $2,918) and the median family income was $103,060 (+/− $3,429). Males had a median income of $66,178 (+/− $2,448) versus $54,733 (+/− $2,427) for females. The [[per capita income]] for the borough was $40,036 (+/− $1,203). About 3.2% of families and 5.3% of the population were below the [[poverty line]], including 7.9% of those under age 18 and 4.8% of those age 65 or over.[http://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/10_5YR/DP03/0600000US3403524900 DP03: Selected Economic Characteristics from the 2006-2010 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates for Franklin Township, Somerset County, New Jersey] {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20200212083236/http://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/10_5YR/DP03/0600000US3403524900 |date=2020-02-12 }}, [[United States Census Bureau]]. Accessed October 18, 2017. ==Historic district== The [[Kingston Mill Historic District]] is a {{convert|49|acre|adj=on}} [[historic district (United States)|historic district]] encompassing the community of [[Kingston, New Jersey]] (which is bounded by Franklin Township in [[Somerset County, New Jersey|Somerset County]], [[Princeton, New Jersey|Princeton]] in [[Mercer County, New Jersey|Mercer County]], and [[South Brunswick, New Jersey|South Brunswick]] in [[Middlesex County, New Jersey|Middlesex County]]). In 1683, Henry Greenland built the first tavern here for travelers between [[New York City]] and [[Philadelphia]]. The current '''Kingston Mill''', also known as the '''Kingston Gristmill''', was built in 1888, the third one at this site. In 1755, Jacob Skilman built a gristmill and sawmill here on the [[Millstone River]], located along the historic [[King's Highway (Charleston to Boston)|King's Highway]]. It was added to the [[National Register of Historic Places]] on April 10, 1986 for its significance in engineering, exploration/settlement, industry, and transportation.
